docs.text:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate            # Windows
source .venv/bin/activate         # macOS / Linux
pip install -e ".[desktop]"       # drop [desktop] for a headless/server install

Python 3.11 or newer is required. You can also download a standalone build from Releases, which needs no Python (see DEPLOYMENT).

docs.title: Desktop application
docs.text:
anatele                          # empty window
anatele path/to/flight.tlog      # import and analyse immediately

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Region Contents Menu File (Open Log or Analysis Ctrl+O, Save Analysis As .ant Ctrl+S, Export Report Ctrl+E, Show Original File), Analysis (Re-analyse with the selected profile, Refresh F5), Tools (Profile Editor, Compare With Log, Aircraft Trends), Help (Limitations). Left: Recordings Each imported file shows its status and progress. Analysis runs in a separate worker process, so the window stays responsive. Failed files show the error. Left: Profile The profile you select is attached to the next import (or re-analysis). Profiles are immutable and versioned. Left: Episodes One row per armed episode, showing the phase status (airborne reported, airborne inferred, no airborne evidence, unassessable), takeoff time and crash-report time. Selecting an episode zooms the plots and replay to it. All shows the whole recording. Centre: Plot Selected signals stacked by unit. Dashed lines mark armed, takeoff, crash report and disarmed; the shaded band is the pre-event airborne window. Gaps longer than 5 s are not drawn through. Click a point to open that record in the Evidence tab. Right: X Axis Time from log start, or time from takeoff (for comparing flights). Right: Y Axis Every decoded or derived signal for the selected source. Use the filter box, e.g. vibration, motor., ekf. Bottom tabs Findings · Hypotheses · Rules · Flight Path · Events · Parameters · Missions · Evidence. Double-click any row to see its evidence. Flight Statistics Firmware and semantic pack, frame, record count, takeoff, airborne time, crash report, pre-event vibration, EKF compass ratio, tilt error, motor spread, battery monitoring and top hypothesis.

docs.title: Useful signals
docs.text: Signal Meaning attitude.roll_deg, attitude.pitch_deg, attitude.yaw_deg Estimated attitude attitude.desired_roll_deg, attitude.desired_pitch_deg Controller target (NAV_CONTROLLER_OUTPUT, ATTITUDE_TARGET or ATT Des*) control.tilt_tracking_error_deg Angle between desired and estimated thrust vectors (derived) control.throttle_pct Throttle output (VFR_HUD or CTUN) output.chN Raw servo/ESC PWM motor.N.output_frac, motor.N.at_floor, motor.N.at_ceiling Motor command mapped via SERVOn_FUNCTION and normalised to the PWM range (derived) motor.mix.right_minus_left, front_minus_back, ccw_minus_cw Mixer decomposition of the motor commands (derived) imu.N.vibration.{x,y,z}, imu.N.clipping_counter Vibration and clipping ekf.compass_ratio, ekf.velocity_ratio, ekf.core*.… EKF innovation test ratios gps.fix_type, gps.h_acc_m GPS quality position.altitude_home, position.latitude, position.longitude Estimated position battery.voltage, battery.current Only when a monitor reports non-zero values

docs.title: Flight Path tab
docs.text:
• The 3D path shows the recorded estimated position in metres east/north/up, relative to the first fix of the episode.
  • The path colour shows the flight mode (AUTO, RTL, LAND …). The grey line is the ground shadow.
  • Waypoint colours: green = reported complete, yellow-green = within radius plus GPS accuracy, amber = completion not observed, red = not visited.
  • X markers: takeoff, attitude excursion, crash report and disarmed.
  • Play animates the aircraft; the red arms are the front. Drag with the mouse to rotate the view.
  • Export GIF… saves an animation, or a still image if you choose .png.

docs.title: Comparing and trending
docs.text:
• Parameters tab → Compare against → Diff: typed differences against another log or the attached profile. Raw-only differences (unverified encoding) are listed separately.
  • Tools → Compare With Log: metrics from the pre-event airborne window side by side, rule states and the parameter diff.
  • Tools → Aircraft Trends: every analysed flight uploaded with a profile of that aircraft key, with a chart of vibration, compass ratio and motor spread over time.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
anatele                         desktop app
anatele web [--port 8766]       web UI on 127.0.0.1
anatele analyse LOG [--json]    findings, hypotheses and rule summary in the terminal (LOG may be a .ant)
anatele export LOG [-o F.ant] [--include-original]   analyse and save a shareable .ant
anatele replay LOG [--out x.gif|x.png] [--episode N] [--fps 12] [--seconds 12]
anatele simulate [--scenario NAME|all] [--out DIR|file.tlog] [--seed N] [--duration S]

Example:

$ anatele analyse simulations/sim_motor_failure.tlog
sim_motor_failure.tlog: 5,387 records, status complete
  source 1:1        vehicle              arducopter-4.7.2
  episode 0: airborne_inferred, takeoff 23.3s, crash report 71.4s

Findings:
  [critical] Crash-check disarm reported
  [critical] Sustained attitude (tilt) tracking error before upset
  [warning ] Motor command at ceiling before upset
  [warning ] Motor output imbalance before event
  ...
Hypotheses for episode 0 (screening order, not probability):
  1. Mechanical/thrust-generation or frame configuration problem — strong support
  ...

docs.title: Flight simulator
docs.text:
anatele simulate --out simulations                  # all five scenarios
anatele simulate --scenario compass_interference --out compass.tlog --seed 7
Scenario What happens What AnaTele should show nominal Arm, AUTO takeoff, 4 waypoints, RTL, land No critical findings; all waypoints reported_complete motor_failure Motor 3's thrust degrades mid-mission until the controller saturates and the crash check disarms Tracking loss, motor ceiling and imbalance, thrust hypothesis ranked first; later waypoints not visited compass_interference Motor current corrupts the magnetometer, causing yaw error, toilet-bowling during RTL and a compass switch EKF compass ratio above 1 pre-event, compass-selection event, circling path in the replay vibration Damaged propeller Sustained vibration above 30 m/s², clipping increments before the event radio_failsafe PreArm radio warnings, then RC loss mid-mission and RTL PreArm radio finding, RTL mode change, waypoints after the loss not visited

The physics is deliberately simple: a rigid quad, an ArduPilot-style roll/pitch-over-yaw mixer priority, linear drag and wind. Output is labelled SIMULATED FLIGHT inside the log and is located at the public SITL default field. Use it to learn the tool, test rules and reproduce patterns. It does not prove anything about a real aircraft.

docs.title: Aircraft profiles
docs.text:
Tools → Profile Editor (or POST /api/profiles):

Field Use Aircraft key Stable id such as quad-01. Saving again creates version 2, 3, … Name, frame, firmware, notes Operator declarations, shown in reports. They are not verified against the binary. Vibration screening Threshold used by the vibration rules (default 30 m/s²) Expected parameters NAME=value per line. Checked by profile-parameter-mismatch and the parameter diff.

Attach the profile before importing. Existing analyses are never rewritten; use Analysis → Re-analyse.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: File → Export Report (or /api/logs/{id}/report) writes a self-contained HTML file with the file hash, engine/rule/semantic versions, phases, ranked hypotheses, findings with evidence ids, the full rule-coverage table, mission item statuses and limitations. Print it to PDF from a browser.

docs.title: Sharing analyses (.ant)
docs.text:
An .ant file (ANalysed Telemetry) is a finished AnaTele analysis that someone else can open without re-running anything: findings, ranked hypotheses, rule coverage, phases, missions, flight statistics, every plot and the 3D flight path.

How Save Open Desktop File → Save Analysis As (.ant) Ctrl+S File → Open Ctrl+O, or anatele shared.ant Web Save analysis (.ant) link above the results Choose the .ant in the upload box CLI anatele export LOG -o flight.ant anatele analyse flight.ant

When saving you choose:

  • Analysis only (default): smaller. The recipient sees decoded records but not raw bytes, and cannot re-analyse.
  • Include original log: embeds the untouched log so the recipient can view raw bytes and re-analyse with a newer engine or their own profile.

Both contain GPS positions and timestamps of the flight. Share only with people you trust.

What's inside. An .ant is a ZIP container (like .docx), so unzip -l flight.ant works:

Entry Contents mimetype application/vnd.anatele.analysis+zip (first, uncompressed) meta.json Format version, AnaTele/engine/rule-pack versions, original filename/size/SHA-256, profile snapshot, SHA-256 of every entry manifest.json The full analysis result observations.parquet, signals.parquet Decoded records and normalised signals report.html The printable report, readable without AnaTele original.tlog / .bin / .log / .csv Only with Include original log

Safety. Opening an .ant never runs analysis or code from the file. AnaTele accepts only the entries above, caps sizes while extracting (1 GiB file, 768 MiB per Parquet, 100 MiB original), rejects encrypted entries, and verifies every SHA-256 and the Parquet schema before registering it. Altered or damaged files are refused. Hashes prove the content is internally consistent, not who made it. An imported analysis shows shared analysis from … in the report and status line, and keeps the engine version it was produced with.

docs.title: Investigating a crash: a worked example
docs.text:
1. Import the log with the aircraft's profile attached.
  2. Check Flight Statistics: was the firmware matched? Is battery monitoring present? Was takeoff reported or inferred?
  3. In Episodes, select the crash episode. Plot roll, pitch and control.tilt_tracking_error_deg. When did tracking first diverge, relative to the shaded pre-event window?
  4. Add motor.*.output_frac. Did one motor go to ceiling or floor first? Is the imbalance mostly in yaw (motor.mix.ccw_minus_cw)?
  5. Add ekf.compass_ratio and imu.0.vibration.z. Were they elevated before the upset, or only at impact?
  6. Read Hypotheses. Each one lists its supporting and contradicting rules and the observation that would separate it from the others.
  7. Open Flight Path to see where the upset began relative to the mission, and which waypoints were reached.
  8. Export the report. Follow up with the onboard .bin log and a safe, props-off inspection; don't fly another Auto mission.

docs.title: Tips and troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Explanation airborne inferred instead of reported The capture has no EXTENDED_SYS_STATE. Takeoff was inferred from altitude rise with demand. Many rules unassessable The needed messages weren't streamed or recorded, or the sample rate is too low for the persistence criterion. Use the onboard .bin log. Parameters shown as raw … (unverified) The integer encoding couldn't be confirmed (non-ArduPilot autopilot, or capabilities missing). Power-related causes cannot be assessed SYS_STATUS reported 0 V, meaning no battery monitor is configured. Older analyses lack phases and rules They were made with an earlier engine. Use Analysis → Re-analyse. Analysis stopped after 180 s The file is too large for the local deadline. Split it, or raise TIMEOUT_SECONDS in worker.py. Where is my data? See DEPLOYMENT → Data directory.

docs.title: Learn AnaTele from scratch
docs.text:
This is an illustrated course. It assumes no background: you don't need to have flown a drone, opened a log or seen the maths before. By the end you'll be able to read an AnaTele report and explain every number in it.

Every chart is drawn from real data: flights from AnaTele's built-in simulator, analysed by the same code you run. The script that draws them is docs/figures/make_guide_figures.py. Some pages also have small interactive widgets that run in your browser.

Prefer paper?

The same material is available as a printable PDF: AnaTele Illustrated Guide (PDF).

docs.title: How to use this course
docs.text:
• In a hurry? Read chapters 1, 4, 5 and 9. That's enough to read a crash report.
  • Investigating a real crash? Do chapters 4–9 next to the Diagnostics reference.
  • Writing your own rules? Read chapters 8 and 9, then Writing a rule.

The one idea to keep in mind

AnaTele reports observations and hypotheses. It never gives a crash verdict or a probability of cause. If data is missing, the answer is unknown, never fine.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
A quadcopter is four motors with propellers on arms, a battery, and a small computer called the flight controller. AnaTele works with flight controllers running ArduPilot, the open-source autopilot used in everything from hobby quads to survey drones.

ArduPilot numbers the motors of an "X" quad the way the figure shows. Motor 1 is front-right, not front-left, which surprises most people. Diagonal pairs spin the same way: M1 and M2 counter-clockwise (CCW), M3 and M4 clockwise (CW). Each spinning propeller twists the frame the opposite way. With two of each direction, the twists cancel and the drone doesn't spin.

Why this matters in an investigation

If a motor is wired to the wrong output, or a propeller is on the wrong motor, the drone usually flips on takeoff. AnaTele reads SERVOn_FUNCTION, FRAME_CLASS and FRAME_TYPE from the log so that every motor number it shows matches this picture.

docs.title: Three angles: roll, pitch, yaw
docs.text:
The attitude of a drone is which way it's facing and how it's tilted. Three angles describe it:

  • Roll: tilting left or right, like a plane banking.
  • Pitch: nose up or nose down.
  • Yaw: turning left or right while staying level. This is the drone's heading.

A quadcopter has no rudder or wings, so it moves by tilting. To fly forward it pitches its nose down. Part of the thrust then points backwards and pushes it forward. That is why "is the tilt correct?" is the most important question in chapter 5.

docs.title: Thrust, weight and hover
docs.text:
To hover, the motors must push up exactly as hard as gravity pulls down.

The simulator's drone weighs 1.6 kg, so its weight is

\[ W = m g = 1.6\,\text{kg} \times 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \approx 15.7\,\text{N}. \]

ArduPilot records the motor output needed to hover as MOT_THST_HOVER. In the simulated flights it is 0.38: 38 % of the usable range. More output gives more thrust and the drone climbs. Less output and it descends.

Motors also have limits. Below MOT_SPIN_MIN (0.15 here) they can stall. Above MOT_SPIN_MAX (0.95) there's no headroom left. A motor that sits at one of these limits is saturated. Chapter 6 shows why that's an important clue.

Check your understanding

The drone is hovering and you want it to roll right. Which motors must push harder?

Answer

The left ones (M2 back-left and M3 front-left). Pushing up harder on the left tips the drone to the right.

docs.title: What is a flight log?
docs.text:
During a flight, the flight controller reads its sensors hundreds of times a second. It estimates where it is, decides what to do and drives the motors. It also writes a record of all of this, and that record is the flight log.

There are two kinds, and AnaTele reads both:

Log Where it is made What it contains Telemetry log .tlog On the ground station (e.g. Mission Planner), from the radio link MAVLink messages, each stamped with the time the ground received it DataFlash log .bin / .log On the drone's SD card ArduPilot's own on-board records; usually higher rate and more detail

MAVLink is the language drones and ground stations use to talk. Each MAVLink message has a type (for example ATTITUDE or GPS_RAW_INT) and named fields (roll, pitch, lat, lon…).

docs.title: A log is a stream of typed messages
docs.text:
Here is the start-to-finish stream of a simulated flight in which one motor fails. Each tick is one message.

Things to notice:

  • ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT and SERVO_OUTPUT_RAW are dense bands: they arrive many times a second.
  • STATUSTEXT (human-readable text such as "Crash: Disarming") shows up only a handful of times, but these messages are often the most important ones.
  • MISSION_ITEM_REACHED marks each waypoint the autopilot reports reaching.

docs.title: Different messages, different rates
docs.text:
In this 102-second simulated .tlog, attitude, position, motor outputs and the controller's targets arrive at 10 Hz (10 times a second). RC input arrives at 5 Hz, and vibration, EKF status, GPS and battery at 2 Hz.

Rate limits what you can conclude

A rule that needs "above 30 for at least 0.5 s" can't be checked properly with data every 0.5 s. AnaTele knows this. When the data is too sparse, it marks the rule unassessable instead of pretending it's healthy (chapter 8).

docs.title: What AnaTele keeps
docs.text: When AnaTele opens a log it keeps every decoded record, with its byte offset in the file. The simulated motor-failure log has 5,387 records. Every chart, threshold and hypothesis in the report can therefore be traced back to the exact bytes it came from. This is the evidence viewer in the desktop app.

docs.title: Two clocks
docs.text:
Every record in a log has a time, but not always from the same clock.

  • Capture time: when the ground station received the message (the 8-byte stamp in front of each .tlog record). It's wall-clock time, so it can jump if the PC's clock is adjusted, and it includes radio delay.
  • Boot time (time_boot_ms, time_usec): how long the flight controller has been powered on. It's precise, but it restarts from zero when the board reboots.

docs.title: Epochs
docs.text:
If the board reboots mid-log, "10 s after boot" happens twice. Put both runs on one timeline and you'd mix two different flights. AnaTele avoids this by splitting the log into epochs. A new epoch starts whenever a clock clearly goes backwards. Inside one epoch, time only moves forward, so samples can be ordered, paired and compared safely.

The exact tests (per source) are:

Clock New epoch when… Why the margin .tlog boot time time_boot_ms it drops by more than 10 s Small regressions are just reordered / delayed packets DataFlash boot time it drops by more than 1 s On-board records are written in order .tlog capture time it drops by more than 2 s PC clock adjustments separate the whole capture

A boot-time drop from near \(2^{32}\) ms back to near zero is recognised as a counter wrap (after ~49.7 days), not a reboot. Every epoch split is listed as a diagnostic, so you can see why it happened.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: A capture can hold messages from more than one system: the drone, a gimbal, the ground station, a companion computer. MAVLink identifies each sender by a system id and component id. AnaTele calls each pair a source (for example 1:1 is the autopilot) and never mixes signals from different sources.

docs.title: Pairing samples
docs.text:
Many checks compare two signals, for example desired and actual roll. They don't arrive at exactly the same instant, so AnaTele pairs each sample with the nearest sample of the other signal, within a tolerance. For attitude that tolerance is 0.25 s. If no partner is close enough, the pair is skipped rather than guessed.

Design principle

Nothing is interpolated or invented. A derived value always comes from real samples, close enough in time to be compared, and it keeps a link to the record it came from.

docs.title: 4. Flight phases
docs.text:
A crash investigation is about timing: what was normal, when did it stop being normal, what came first. So the first thing AnaTele does with each armed period (an episode) is split it into phases.

In the nominal simulated flight, the drone arms at 20.0 s and AnaTele finds takeoff at 23.29 s. It's airborne until 91.09 s and disarms at 94.27 s.

docs.title: Step 1: the armed baseline
docs.text: Altitude estimates drift, so "altitude = 0" doesn't reliably mean "on the ground". AnaTele takes the median home-relative altitude during the first 2 s after arming as the ground level (the baseline). The median is used instead of the mean so a single bad sample can't move it.

docs.title: Step 2: confirm, then backtrack
docs.text:
1. Find the first sample at least 1.0 m above the baseline. That is clearly flying, not noise.
  2. Check that there was real demand in the 5 s before it: throttle at least 10 %, or (if throttle isn't logged) a motor output of at least 25 % of its range. If the altitude rose with no demand, it's treated as estimate drift and the drone is not considered airborne.
  3. Walk backwards to the last sample still within 0.2 m of the baseline. That's the takeoff time, T+0.

If the autopilot itself reports "Taking off" or "In air" (a landed-state message), AnaTele uses that instead and labels the phase reported rather than inferred.

docs.title: Step 3: the pre-event window
docs.text:
Rules mostly look at the time before anything went wrong. Once the drone has hit the ground, all the sensors go wild, and that's a consequence, not a cause.

The window ends at the earliest of:

  • the first moment roll or pitch exceeds 60° (an attitude excursion, i.e. loss of control);
  • 3 s before an autopilot crash report (the event guard);
  • the last sample at least 0.5 m above the baseline.

In the motor-failure flight, ArduPilot reported "Crash: Disarming: AngErr=31>30" at 71.37 s. The roll and pitch never passed 60°, so the pre-event window runs from takeoff (23.29 s) to 68.37 s, exactly 3 s before the report.

Phase labels in the report

  • airborne_reported: from the autopilot's own landed-state messages.
  • airborne_inferred: from altitude rise plus demand, as above.
  • no_airborne_evidence: armed, but never clearly flew.
  • unassessable: no altitude data, so we can't tell.

docs.title: Desired versus actual
docs.text:
The autopilot constantly decides what attitude it wants (desired roll and pitch). It then tries to achieve it with the motors. A healthy drone follows closely:

When a motor is failing, a propeller is damaged or the frame is wrongly configured, the drone can no longer follow. The gap between "wanted" and "got" grows. This is one of the strongest clues in an investigation.

docs.title: One number: the tilt error
docs.text:
Roll and pitch errors could be checked separately, but what really matters is which way the thrust points. So AnaTele turns each (roll, pitch) pair into a unit vector along the drone's thrust axis:

\[ \hat{t}(\phi, \theta) = \big( \sin\theta \cos\phi,\; -\sin\phi,\; \cos\theta \cos\phi \big) \]

where \(\phi\) is roll and \(\theta\) is pitch. The tilt error is the angle between the desired and actual vectors:

\[ e = \arccos\!\big( \hat{t}_\text{desired} \cdot \hat{t}_\text{actual} \big). \]

Desired and actual samples are paired with the nearest-in-time rule from chapter 3 (within 0.25 s).

docs.title: What it looks like in a failure
docs.text:
In the nominal flight the tilt error never exceeds 23.4°, during brisk turns. In the motor-failure flight it first passes 30° at 51.99 s and peaks at 48.4° before the event window ends. The longest stretch above 30° lasts 1.6 s. The tracking-loss rule needs 30° for at least 0.5 s, so it is triggered.

Tilt error is a symptom, not a cause

A large tilt error says "the drone could not do what it was told". It doesn't say why. A weak motor, a loose prop, the wrong frame type, a very aggressive tune or a strong gust can all cause it. AnaTele uses it as evidence for the thrust/configuration hypothesis (chapter 9), together with the motor signals in chapter 6.

docs.title: The mixer
docs.text:
The pilot or autopilot asks for four things: throttle (up/down), roll, pitch and yaw. The mixer turns these into one command per motor.

For each motor at arm position \((x, y)\) (right, forward) with spin \(s\) (+1 for CCW, −1 for CW), the command is roughly

\[ u_i = \text{throttle} \;-\; x_i\,\text{roll} \;+\; y_i\,\text{pitch} \;+\; s_i\,\text{yaw}. \]

Each command must stay between MOT_SPIN_MIN and MOT_SPIN_MAX. If the sum doesn't fit, ArduPilot (and AnaTele's simulator) keeps roll and pitch, because they keep the drone upright, and gives up yaw first.

Try it: push the roll slider until one motor hits a limit.

docs.title: Healthy motors
docs.text: In the nominal flight all four commands move together around a mean of about 1383 µs while airborne. They spread apart briefly in turns and accelerations.

docs.title: A failing motor
docs.text:
In the motor-failure scenario, the simulator makes motor 3 lose thrust. Its health falls as \(h_3 = \max(0.3,\; 1 - 0.06\,(t - t_f))\) from \(t_f = 40.85\) s. The autopilot doesn't know this. It only sees the drone tilting the wrong way, so it commands motor 3 harder and the opposite motor (4) softer.

Read this the right way round

The motor with the highest command is often the weak one. The controller is trying to make up for missing thrust. A log records commands, not thrust, so AnaTele says "command anomaly", never "motor 3 failed".

docs.title: Saturation
docs.text:
A motor is at ceiling if its PWM is within 2 µs of the ceiling, and at floor if within 2 µs of the floor. The limits come from the log's own parameters:

\[ \text{floor} = \text{PWM}_\text{min} + \text{SPIN}_\text{min}\,(\text{PWM}_\text{max} - \text{PWM}_\text{min}) \] \[ \text{ceiling} = \text{PWM}_\text{min} + \text{SPIN}_\text{max}\,(\text{PWM}_\text{max} - \text{PWM}_\text{min}) \]

With 1000–2000 µs and spin limits 0.15/0.95, that's 1150 µs and 1950 µs.

Before the event, motor 3 spends 31.6 % of the airborne samples at its ceiling. Its longest unbroken stretch is 2.2 s. The motor-ceiling-saturation rule needs at least 1 s, so it's triggered. No motor stays at the floor for 2 s, so motor-floor-saturation-pre-event is not triggered.

docs.title: Imbalance
docs.text: AnaTele also averages each motor's command over the pre-event window (as a fraction of the PWM range). In the failure flight the means are M1 0.47, M2 0.47, M3 0.65, M4 0.34: a spread of 0.31, above the 0.12 screening limit. motor-output-imbalance-pre-event is triggered. Wind, payload offset and yaw demand can also cause imbalance, and the report says so.

docs.title: Vibration
docs.text:
The accelerometers measure acceleration, which the autopilot needs to know which way is down. A damaged propeller, loose motor or stiff mounting adds shaking that the accelerometers also pick up. Too much of it and the position and altitude estimates degrade.

ArduPilot logs vibration levels in m/s² for each axis. Its own guidance treats 30 as worth looking at and 60 as bad.

Flight Peak vibration Longest run above 30 m/s² (pre-event) Rule nominal 15.7 m/s² 0 s not triggered vibration (damaged prop) 54.9 m/s² 12.5 s on z triggered

vibration-persistent-pre-event triggers if any axis stays above 30 for 2 s or above 60 for 1 s. The damaged-prop flight also logged 283 accelerometer clipping events, where the sensor hit its maximum, so clipping-pre-event triggers too.

docs.title: The EKF: the autopilot's best guess
docs.text:
ArduPilot fuses all its sensors in an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). For each sensor it predicts what the next reading should be, then compares that with the actual reading. The gap, scaled by how big a gap it expects, is the test ratio:

\[ \text{ratio} = \frac{\text{innovation}^2}{\text{expected variance}} \quad\text{(reported so that } 1.0 = \text{at the limit).} \]

Below 1 means the sensor agrees with the filter. Above 1 means the EKF is starting to distrust it.

docs.title: Compass interference
docs.text:
High motor currents create magnetic fields. If the compass sits too close to the power wires, its heading shifts whenever the motors work hard.

In the compass-interference flight, the EKF compass ratio reached 2.07. Before the event it stayed above 1.0 for 24.5 s in one run. ekf-compass-innovation-pre-event needs above 1.0 for 2 s, so it's triggered.

When the heading is wrong, the drone flies in curving, growing circles ("toilet-bowling"). The autopilot steers for where it thinks it's facing, not where it actually is.

Why a 'compasses inconsistent' message after a crash proves little

After the motor-failure crash, the simulator (like real ArduPilot) printed "PreArm: Compasses inconsistent". A crash can bend a compass mount, so this message comes after the incident. AnaTele records it (compasses-inconsistent-reported) but gives it little weight.

docs.title: What a rule is
docs.text: A rule is a small, versioned, written-down check: "if this signal stays above this threshold for this long, during this phase, report it". All rules live in one file, the rule pack (telemetry_platform/rules/core.yaml). Every report records which pack version and SHA-256 it used, so the same log always gives the same answer.

docs.title: Persistence: ignore blips, catch trends
docs.text:
Real signals are noisy. A single spike is usually meaningless, so most rules need a run: consecutive samples above the threshold, lasting at least for_s seconds. Two more details:

  • If two samples are too far apart (more than the maximum gap), the run is broken. AnaTele doesn't assume what happened in between.
  • A run's length is measured from its first to its last sample above the threshold.

Try it, including what happens when data gets sparse:

docs.title: The four states
docs.text:
State Meaning triggered The data is there and the condition was met. not triggered The data is there and the condition was not met. unassessable The data needed is missing, or too sparse to decide. Not the same as healthy. not applicable The rule doesn't apply here, e.g. a profile check when no profile was selected.

Here are real examples from the simulated flights:

Unknown is never healthy

Many tools show a green tick when a check couldn't run. AnaTele never does. If a log has no vibration data, the vibration rules say unassessable, and any hypothesis that depends on them says so too.

docs.title: Counting the five simulated flights
docs.text:
Flight triggered not triggered not applicable nominal 1 19 2 motor_failure 7 14 1 compass_interference 2 18 2 vibration 5 15 2 radio_failsafe 2 18 2

The one rule that triggers even in the nominal flight is fs-gcs-disabled. It's a configuration observation (the ground-station failsafe is turned off), not a fault. That's why rules have severities and are kept separate from hypotheses.

docs.title: 9. Hypotheses
docs.text: Rules say what was observed. Hypotheses ask what could explain it. AnaTele ranks the hypotheses only for episodes that end in a critical event (an autopilot crash report). In the five simulated flights that's only the motor-failure flight.

docs.title: The four built-in hypotheses
docs.text: Hypothesis Supported by (family, weight) Counted against it Mechanical / thrust or frame configuration tracking-loss (control, 1) · motor floor saturation (propulsion, 1) · motor imbalance (propulsion, 0.75) · motor ceiling saturation (propulsion, 0.5) – Estimator / magnetic inconsistency compass event before crash check (estimator, 1) · EKF compass innovation (magnetic, 1) · compasses inconsistent reported (magnetic, 0.25) compass event flagged as coming after the upset (1) Vibration-driven estimation degradation persistent vibration (inertial, 1) · clipping (inertial, 1) vibration checked and fine (0.5) · clipping checked and fine (0.5) Electrical / power degradation no support rules yet in this pack version blocked if power-monitoring-gap fires

docs.title: The score
docs.text:
\[ \text{score} = \sum_{\text{families } f} \min\!\Big(1.5,\; \sum_{\text{triggered rules in } f} w\Big) \;-\; \sum_{\text{contradictions}} w \]

The family cap of 1.5 matters. Three rules that all measure motor commands are not three independent pieces of evidence. Capping each family stops one kind of evidence from dominating. Evidence from different families (say, control and propulsion) does add up.

Label When strong support score ≥ 2 some support score ≥ 1 weak support score > 0 mixed support there is both support and contradiction limited or contradicting evidence score ≤ 0 unassessable none of its rules could be checked (or a blocking rule fired)

docs.title: Worked example: the motor-failure flight
docs.text:
• Thrust/configuration: control family = 1 (tracking-loss). Propulsion family = 0.75 + 0.5 = 1.25 (imbalance + ceiling), under the cap. Score = 1 + 1.25 = 2.25, so strong support.
  • Vibration: nothing triggered, and both vibration rules were checked and fine, giving −0.5 − 0.5 = −1.0: limited or contradicting evidence. Checking and finding nothing counts against an explanation.
  • Magnetic: score 0. The post-crash "Compasses inconsistent" message doesn't count, because it isn't from the flight's own time window.
  • Power: unassessable. The current pack has no rule that can support it, so it's listed as a reminder of what the log can't tell you. Confirming it needs battery voltage/current logs.

Toggle the evidence yourself:

This is a screening order, not a probability

A score of 2.25 doesn't mean "90 % likely". The weights are written-down expert judgements, and the list tells you what to inspect first. Each hypothesis also lists the discriminating evidence that would confirm or rule it out. For thrust problems that's ESC RPM/current telemetry, a props-off motor test and a physical inspection.

docs.title: Where did it go?
docs.text:
An AUTO mission is a list of numbered items, usually waypoints (latitude, longitude, altitude). The ground station uploads them, the autopilot flies them in order and reports MISSION_ITEM_REACHED as it gets to each one.

AnaTele rebuilds the uploaded plan from the log's own messages. Then, for each waypoint, it checks whether the drone actually got there.

The simulated mission is a takeoff to 10 m, four waypoints and a return-to-launch. In the nominal flight every waypoint is reported reached. In the motor-failure flight:

Item Status Nearest recorded position WP2–WP4 reported_complete 0.97, 0.97, 0.70 m WP5 geometry_consistent_with_completion 0.32 m, but no "reached" report before the crash RTL completion_not_observed (not a positional item)

docs.title: Distance on a sphere
docs.text:
GPS gives latitude and longitude in degrees, but we need metres. On a sphere of radius \(R\), the shortest distance between two points is along the surface. The haversine formula gives it:

\[ h = \sin^2\!\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2} + \cos\varphi_1 \cos\varphi_2 \sin^2\!\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}, \qquad d = 2R \arcsin\sqrt{h} \]

with \(\varphi\) = latitude, \(\lambda\) = longitude (in radians) and \(R = 6\,371\,008.8\) m (the mean Earth radius).

Over a few kilometres the flat-earth shortcut is accurate to millimetres, far smaller than GPS error. AnaTele uses haversine anyway because it's correct everywhere, including long survey flights and high latitudes.

docs.title: When does a waypoint count as reached?
docs.text:
ArduPilot treats a waypoint as reached when the drone is within WP_RADIUS_M (2 m in the simulation). GPS has its own uncertainty, so AnaTele allows

\[ d_\text{nearest} \le \texttt{WP\_RADIUS\_M} + h_\text{acc} \]

where \(h_\text{acc}\) is the GPS horizontal accuracy at that moment. Passing this test is labelled consistent with completion, not completed: being close isn't proof.

docs.title: Drawing the path
docs.text:
The 3D replay in the desktop app draws the flown path with the waypoints. To keep drawing fast it uses at most 6,000 points, keeping every k-th sample with \(k = \lceil n / 6000 \rceil\):

Note

Thinning only affects the picture. Every rule, statistic and distance above uses every sample.

docs.title: 11. The simulator
docs.text:
Every chart in this course came from AnaTele's built-in flight simulator. It exists so that you can learn and test without crashing a real drone. Each scenario has a known cause, so you can check that the analysis finds it.

anatele simulate --out simulations          # all five scenarios
anatele simulations/sim_motor_failure.tlog  # analyse one

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every 10 ms the simulator:

  1. Guidance picks a target velocity towards the active waypoint.
  2. Attitude control turns that into desired roll and pitch (capped at 0.52 rad ≈ 30°), and a yaw target.
  3. The mixer (chapter 6) turns throttle and torques into four motor commands between 0.15 and 0.95.
  4. Physics turns commands into thrust and torque. It then integrates Newton's laws for a 1.6 kg quad with 0.18 m arms, drag and a gusting wind.
  5. Sensors and MAVLink: every 100 ms it writes ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT, SERVO_OUTPUT_RAW and more (and slower health messages every 500 ms) into a genuine .tlog, byte for byte as Mission Planner would.

The thrust per motor is

\[ F_i = h_i \cdot F_\text{max} \cdot u_i, \qquad F_\text{max} = \frac{m g}{4 \cdot 0.38} \approx 10.3\ \text{N}, \]

so at the hover output 0.38, four healthy motors exactly hold the weight. \(h_i\) is the motor's health (1 = perfect).

docs.title: The five scenarios
docs.text:
Scenario What is injected What AnaTele finds nominal nothing only the configuration note fs-gcs-disabled motor_failure motor 3 health \(\max(0.3, 1 - 0.06(t - t_f))\) from 2 s after WP3 becomes active tracking loss, ceiling saturation, imbalance; thrust/configuration: strong support compass_interference heading error that grows with motor current EKF compass innovation above 1 for 24.5 s vibration random torque noise (a damaged prop) persistent vibration, 283 clips radio_failsafe RC signal lost mid-mission pre-arm radio failsafe reports

Make your own

Simulator(scenario, seed, mission=[...], wind=(n, e)) in telemetry_platform/simulator.py takes your own mission and wind. Different seeds give different noise but the same physics.

Warning

The simulator is a teaching and testing model, not a certified flight dynamics model. Real crashes are messier. Use it to understand the method, not to calibrate thresholds for a real aircraft.

docs.title: 12. Sharing with .ant files
docs.text: An investigation is often a team effort. The pilot, the builder and a reviewer may all need to see the same thing. Instead of sending a raw log and hoping everyone uses the same version of every tool, AnaTele saves the whole analysis as one file: .ant.

docs.title: What is inside
docs.text:
An .ant is an ordinary ZIP file. You can open it with any unzip tool, but AnaTele checks it strictly:

  1. mimetype must be exactly application/vnd.anatele.analysis+zip.
  2. meta.json lists the SHA-256 hash of every other entry. A SHA-256 hash is a 64-character fingerprint: change one byte of a file and the fingerprint changes completely.
  3. Each entry is size-limited, hashed and compared. The JSON and Parquet structure is validated before anything is shown.

Any mismatch and the file is rejected. A modified analysis can't pass as the original.

docs.title: Saving and opening
docs.text:
DesktopCommand lineWeb / API

File → Save Analysis As (.ant) (Ctrl+S). Open with File → Open or drag and drop.

anatele export flight.tlog -o flight.ant            # analysis only
anatele export flight.tlog -o flight.ant --include-original
anatele analyse flight.ant                           # print the summary

GET /api/logs/{id}/export.ant to download, POST /api/analyses to import.

Privacy

--include-original embeds the untouched log, and that contains GPS positions (where you fly, often where you live). Leave it out unless the receiver needs to re-run the analysis or inspect raw bytes.

docs.title: The report inside
docs.text:
report.html is a self-contained, printable report: findings, hypotheses, rule states, phases and the mission table. It opens in any browser, so someone without AnaTele can still read the result.

You've finished the course. Next: open a real log in the desktop app, use the Usage guide for the controls and the Diagnostics reference for every rule.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning ArduPilot Open-source autopilot firmware for drones, planes, rovers and boats. Armed Motors are allowed to spin. An episode is one armed period. Attitude Orientation of the drone: roll, pitch and yaw. Baseline altitude Median altitude over the first 2 s after arming, treated as "ground". Ceiling / floor The highest / lowest motor command allowed (MOT_SPIN_MAX / MOT_SPIN_MIN). Clipping An accelerometer reading hit the sensor's maximum, so the true value is unknown. DataFlash log On-board log (.bin/.log) written to the flight controller's SD card. EKF Extended Kalman Filter, ArduPilot's sensor-fusion estimator. Epoch A stretch of a log in which the clock only moves forward (split at reboots). Event guard The pre-event window ends 3 s before an autopilot crash report. Family (evidence) A group of related rules; its contribution to a hypothesis is capped at 1.5. Haversine Formula for distance between two latitude/longitude points on a sphere. Hypothesis A possible explanation, scored by evidence for and against. Not a probability. Innovation / test ratio How far a sensor reading is from the EKF's prediction, scaled so 1.0 is the limit. MAVLink The message protocol between drones and ground stations. Mixer Turns throttle/roll/pitch/yaw demands into individual motor commands. Persistence A condition must hold continuously for a minimum time to count. Pre-event window From takeoff to just before the upset or crash report; where rules look for causes. PWM Pulse width (µs) sent to a motor controller; here 1000 = off, 2000 = full. Rule pack The versioned YAML file of all rules and hypotheses. Rule state triggered / not triggered / unassessable / not applicable. Saturation A motor stuck at its ceiling or floor, so the controller has no headroom left. Source One MAVLink sender (system id : component id), e.g. 1:1. STATUSTEXT Human-readable text messages from the autopilot (e.g. "Crash: Disarming"). Tilt error Angle between desired and actual thrust direction. .tlog Telemetry log saved by the ground station from the radio link. .ant AnaTele's shareable, hash-verified analysis file. Unassessable The data needed to check something is missing or too sparse. Never "healthy". WP_RADIUS_M How close the drone must get for a waypoint to count as reached.

docs.title: Interactive widgets
docs.text: These small widgets let you try the ideas behind an AnaTele report yourself. Each one uses the same formulas and thresholds as the analysis code, so the numbers you see here match what AnaTele would compute. They run entirely in your browser and do not send data anywhere.

docs.title: Tilt tracking error
docs.text: A multicopter steers by leaning its thrust. AnaTele compares the lean the controller asked for with the lean the estimator reported. It turns each roll/pitch pair into a unit "thrust direction" and measures the angle between the two. That way roll and pitch errors combine into one number. The tracking-loss rule fires when this angle stays above 30° for at least 0.5 s.

docs.title: Motor mixer (QUAD/X)
docs.text: The mixer turns throttle, roll, pitch and yaw demands into four motor commands. On a QUAD/X frame, motors 1 (front right) and 2 (back left) spin counter-clockwise, and motors 3 (front left) and 4 (back right) spin clockwise. Each output must stay between MOT_SPIN_MIN and MOT_SPIN_MAX. When it can't, the mixer protects roll and pitch first and gives up yaw. A motor stuck at its floor or ceiling is something AnaTele flags as evidence.

docs.title: Persistence: threshold plus duration
docs.text: One spiky sample does not mean anything is wrong, so most AnaTele rules need a signal to stay above a threshold for some minimum time. Samples that are too far apart (more than the maximum gap) break a run. If telemetry is too coarse to resolve the required duration, the result is unassessable rather than healthy. Change the rate, gap and dropout to see this happen.

docs.title: Hypothesis screening score
docs.text: Rules that triggered add weight to the hypotheses they support, grouped into evidence families. Each family is capped at 1.5, so many related signals (like three vibration axes) can't pile up. Contradicting findings subtract. The score orders hypotheses for investigation. It is not a probability.

docs.title: Waypoint distance and "reached"
docs.text: AnaTele measures the horizontal distance between a planned waypoint and the closest recorded vehicle position with the haversine (great-circle) formula. It then compares that distance with the acceptance radius (WP_RADIUS_M, 2 m if not logged) plus the GPS accuracy at that moment. Over a few metres a flat-earth calculation gives almost the same answer. Switch the map to 200 km to see the two drift apart.
